profile.feeling: A turn in the sentence: “but”, before anything.

senses.def: but (the light form: before a verb, a noun in the nominative, or any phrase)

examples.text: أَنَا مُتْعَبٌ، لٰكِنْ أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ.
examples.tr: I’m tired, but I’m going to work.
I’d like coffee, but without sugar.

examples.text: أُحِبُّ الشَّايَ وَلٰكِنْ لَا أُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ.
examples.tr: I like tea, but I don’t like coffee.

collocations.tr: but (with “and”: very common at the start of a clause)

synonyms.nuance: but — the heavy form, before a noun in the accusative or a pronoun ending (لٰكِنَّهُ)
however, except that
however

etymology.text: Wiktionary records the light لٰكِنْ as a conjunction of its own (with the derived وَلٰكِن); for the origin of the pair see لٰكِنَّ (uncertain).

funFacts: The long ā is written with a small (dagger) alif over the lām: لٰكِنْ — in everyday print simply لكن, but always pronounced lākin.
pitfalls: Never spelt *لاكن: the ā is the dagger alif, as in هٰذَا and ذٰلِكَ.
Before a noun or pronoun ending you need the heavy لٰكِنَّ: لٰكِنَّهُ جَمِيلٌ.
subtleties: وَلٰكِنْ (“and but”) is the most frequent form at the start of a clause; the وَ adds nothing in English.

profile.feeling: “But” followed by a subject: but it…, but the tea….

senses.def: but (the heavy form: + a noun in the accusative or a pronoun ending)

examples.tr: The house is small, but it is beautiful.
Coffee is expensive, but tea is cheap.
I love the sea, but I don’t swim.

synonyms.nuance: but — the light form, before a verb or anything else

etymology.text: Wiktionary: origin uncertain — Bravmann proposes إِلَّا كَانَ (“except that [it] were”), without explaining the contraction.

funFacts: It is one of the “sisters of إِنَّ” (أَخَوَاتُ إِنَّ) of Arabic grammar: إِنَّ, أَنَّ, لٰكِنَّ … all put their subject in the accusative.
pitfalls: The noun after it is ACCUSATIVE: لٰكِنَّ الشَّايَ رَخِيصٌ, not *لٰكِنَّ الشَّايُ.
A pronoun subject becomes an ending: لٰكِنَّهُ, لٰكِنَّهَا, لٰكِنَّنِي — never *لٰكِنَّ هُوَ.
subtleties: Things in the plural are “she” here too: الْبُيُوتُ صَغِيرَةٌ لٰكِنَّهَا جَمِيلَةٌ.

senses.def: because (+ a noun in the accusative or a pronoun ending)

examples.tr: I don’t drink coffee because it is expensive.
I’m eating now because I’m hungry.

examples.text: لِمَاذَا تَبْقَى فِي الْبَيْتِ؟ لِأَنَّ الْجَوَّ بَارِدٌ.
examples.tr: Why are you staying at home? — Because it is cold.

synonyms.nuance: because of + a noun: بِسَبَبِ الْبَرْدِ, because of the cold
since, as

funFacts: German weil sends the verb to the end of the clause; Arabic لِأَنَّ leaves the order alone but puts the next noun in the accusative.
pitfalls: لِأَنَّ + accusative or a pronoun ending: لِأَنَّ الْجَوَّ بَارِدٌ, لِأَنَّهُ مُتْعَبٌ — not *لِأَنَّ هُوَ مُتْعَبٌ.
“Because of” + noun is بِسَبَبِ, not لِأَنَّ.
subtleties: “I” has two forms: لِأَنَّنِي and the shorter لِأَنِّي; “we”: لِأَنَّنَا or لِأَنَّا.

examples.tr: I’m hungry, so I’m eating.

examples.text: الْجَوُّ بَارِدٌ، لِذٰلِكَ نَبْقَى فِي الْبَيْتِ.
examples.tr: It’s cold, so we’re staying at home.

examples.text: كَانَ الطَّرِيقُ طَوِيلًا، لِذٰلِكَ وَصَلْنَا مُتَأَخِّرِينَ.
examples.tr: The road was long, so we arrived late.

synonyms.nuance: so, that is why — the same with “this”
therefore — the short written form
so, and so — the light prefix: جُعْتُ فَأَكَلْتُ
so then, in that case

funFacts: German deswegen is built the same way (“because of that”), and Greek γι’ αυτό, “for this”.
pitfalls: Spelt with a dagger alif like ذٰلِكَ: لِذٰلِكَ (liḏālika); in print usually لذلك.
No inversion after it (unlike German deshalb + verb): لِذٰلِكَ نَبْقَى فِي الْبَيْتِ is normal order.
subtleties: فَـ is the lighter, more frequent “so”; لِذٰلِكَ states the cause explicitly.

profile.feeling: The tiny link that drives a story on: and so, and then.

senses.def: so, and so, and then (attached to the next word)
then — opening the main clause after إِذَا when it is a command, a negation or a nominal sentence

examples.tr: I got hungry, so I ate.
If you’re hungry, eat!
He came in and sat down.

synonyms.nuance: therefore — a full word, the cause made explicit
then, later — with a pause in time

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the conjunction فَـ, “then, and then; and so, thus, hence, therefore”.

funFacts: Grammarians describe it as order with no delay (ترتيب وتعقيب): فَـ = right after; ثُمَّ = after a while.
pitfalls: It is written joined to the next word: فَأَكَلْتُ, فَكُلْ — never alone.
After إِذَا a command needs it: إِذَا كُنْتَ جَائِعًا فَكُلْ (not *… كُلْ).
subtleties: وَ adds, فَـ follows: أَكَلَ وَشَرِبَ (he ate and drank) / أَكَلَ فَشَبِعَ (he ate and so was full).

examples.text: أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ ثُمَّ أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ.
examples.tr: I drink coffee, then I go to work.
We eat, then we drink tea.
Come in, then sit down.

synonyms.nuance: after that — more explicit
and then — immediately, with no pause

etymology.text: Wiktionary lists it as a conjunction, “then, afterward, subsequently”, also used to mark the speaker’s order of points; no etymology is given.

funFacts: Classical grammar contrasts it with فَـ: ثُمَّ is sequence with a gap in time (ترتيب مع تراخٍ).
pitfalls: ثُمَّ (ṯumma, then) ≠ ثَمَّ / ثَمَّةَ (ṯamma, there; there is) — one vowel.
subtleties: It joins clauses with the same word order as before: أَشْرَبُ … ثُمَّ أَذْهَبُ ….

profile.feeling: Time clauses: when I arrive, when I was a child.

examples.tr: When I get home, I eat.
I drink tea when I’m tired.

examples.text: عِنْدَمَا كُنْتُ طِفْلًا، كُنْتُ أَعِيشُ فِي قَرْيَةٍ.
examples.tr: When I was a child, I lived in a village.

synonyms.nuance: when — for past events (لَمَّا وَصَلْتُ, when I arrived); also the everyday “when” of many dialects
when, at the time when (also حِينَمَا)
when, if — for the future and for general truths

etymology.text: Wiktionary: from عِنْدَ (ʿinda, “at”) + مَا (mā) — “at (the time) that”.

funFacts: It is built from عِنْدَ, the “at” of عِنْدِي (I have, lesson 6): “at what (time)”.
pitfalls: The question “when?” is مَتَى (lesson 10): مَتَى تَصِلُ؟ — عِنْدَمَا only joins two clauses.
To say “to be” in the present after it, use the present of كَانَ: عِنْدَمَا أَكُونُ مُتْعَبًا (and the predicate in the accusative).
subtleties: German distinguishes wenn / als; Arabic عِنْدَمَا covers both, while لَمَّا is only for the past.

examples.tr: When summer comes, we travel.
If you’re hungry, eat!

examples.text: إِذَا كَانَ الْمَطْعَمُ غَالِيًا نَأْكُلُ فِي الْبَيْتِ.
examples.tr: If the restaurant is expensive, we eat at home.

synonyms.nuance: if — a more open or doubtful condition, with the past or the jussive
if — an unreal condition: لَوْ كُنْتُ غَنِيًّا … (if I were rich …); also in لَوْ سَمَحْتَ (lesson 2)

etymology.text: Wiktionary: equivalent to إِن (ʾin, “if”) + ذَا (ḏā, “this”); compare Hebrew אָז (“then”).

funFacts: لَوْ سَمَحْتَ (excuse me, lesson 2) is literally “if you allowed” — the polite unreal “if”.
pitfalls: After إِذَا the verb is normally in the PAST form, but the meaning is present or future: إِذَا ذَهَبْتَ = if you go.
A command, a negation with لَنْ / لَيْسَ or a nominal sentence after it needs فَـ: إِذَا كُنْتَ جَائِعًا فَكُلْ.
For an unreal “if” use لَوْ, not إِذَا.
subtleties: With كَانَ the adjective is accusative: إِذَا كَانَ الْمَطْعَمُ غَالِيًا.

profile.feeling: Reported facts: I know that…, I think that….

senses.def: that (+ a noun in the accusative or a pronoun ending)

examples.tr: I know that you are tired.
I think that the train is fast.
I know that Arabic is difficult.

synonyms.nuance: that + a verb (usually in the subjunctive) — often English “to”
that — after قَالَ (to say): قَالَ إِنَّهُ مُتْعَبٌ

etymology.text: Wiktionary: “adverbial accusative of the noun underlying the former conjunction” (أَنْ); لِأَنَّ (because) is derived from it.

funFacts: Hebrew uses one prefix שֶׁ for this (אֲנִי יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁ…), German dass sends the verb to the end — Arabic أَنَّ changes the case of the subject.
pitfalls: أَنَّ + accusative or a pronoun ending: أَعْرِفُ أَنَّ الْبَيْتَ كَبِيرٌ — after قَالَ it is إِنَّ, not أَنَّ.
أَنَّ (ʾanna, that) and أَنْ (ʾan, that / to) look the same without vowels: أن.
subtleties: أَنِّي and أَنَّنِي (that I) are both correct; أَنَّنِي is more frequent today.

profile.feeling: Wanting and needing to do things: I want to go.

senses.def: that, to (+ a verb in the subjunctive: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ, I want to go)
that (+ a past verb), in reports

examples.tr: I want to drink tea.
We want to travel in the summer.
I must go now.

synonyms.nuance: that + a noun or pronoun ending — facts: أَعْرِفُ أَنَّهُ هُنَا
in order to, so that

etymology.text: Wiktionary: perhaps from the same source as هَمّ (“concern”), with sound changes typical of Arabic (an uncertain proposal); لِأَنْ and أَلَّا (أَنْ + لَا) are derived from it.

funFacts: Greek says it the same way: θέλω να πάω, “I want that I go” = أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ — no infinitive.
pitfalls: The verb after it takes the subjunctive: -a instead of -u (أَنْ أَذْهَبَ, not أَذْهَبُ); the -na of تَأْكُلِينَ / يَأْكُلُونَ drops (أَنْ تَأْكُلِي, أَنْ يَأْكُلُوا).
أَنْ + لَا is written أَلَّا: أُرِيدُ أَلَّا أَذْهَبَ (I want not to go).
subtleties: Where English has “to” (I want to eat), Arabic has أَنْ + a verb with a person: أُرِيدُ أَنْ آكُلَ, تُرِيدُ أَنْ تَأْكُلَ.

profile.feeling: A contrast inside one sentence: although….

senses.def: although, even though (+ a noun in the accusative or a pronoun ending)

examples.text: مَعَ أَنَّنِي مُتْعَبٌ، أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ.
examples.tr: Although I’m tired, I go to work.

examples.text: أَذْهَبُ مَشْيًا مَعَ أَنَّ الْمَدْرَسَةَ بَعِيدَةٌ.
examples.tr: I walk although the school is far.
He bought the car although it is expensive.

synonyms.nuance: although, despite the fact that — very common in writing
in spite of the fact that
despite + a noun

etymology.text: مَعَ (“with”) + أَنَّ (“that”): “with (the fact) that”; Wiktionary lists the pair as a conjunction, “although”.

funFacts: Greek παρόλο που and German obwohl are built from other pieces, but the idea is the same: “with all that, …”.
pitfalls: No لٰكِنْ in the main clause: *مَعَ أَنَّنِي مُتْعَبٌ لٰكِنْ أَذْهَبُ is wrong, like English “although …, but …”.
Like أَنَّ, it takes the accusative or a pronoun ending: مَعَ أَنَّ الْمَدْرَسَةَ بَعِيدَةٌ.
subtleties: The clause can come first or second: مَعَ أَنَّهَا غَالِيَةٌ، اِشْتَرَاهَا / اِشْتَرَاهَا مَعَ أَنَّهَا غَالِيَةٌ.
